variantrule.name: Ability Check
entries: An ability check represents a ship's ability to overcome a challenge. The GM calls for an ability check when a ship, or a crewmember, attempts an action (other than an attack) that has a chance of failure. When the outcome is uncertain, the dice determine the results.

For every ability check, the GM decides which of the 6 abilities is relevant to the task at hand and the difficulty of the task, represented by Difficulty Class. The more difficult a task, the higher its DC. The Typical Difficulty Classes table shows the most common DCs.

To make an ability check, roll a {@dice d20} and add the relevant ability modifier. As with other {@dice d20} rolls, apply bonuses and penalties, and compare the total to the DC. If the total equals or exceeds the DC, the ability check is a success-the ship, or crewmember, overcomes the challenge at hand. Otherwise, it's a failure, which means the ship or crewmember makes no progress toward the objective or makes progress combined with a setback determined by the GM.
When making an ability check that involves your ship's abilities, you use the ship's score instead of your own, as dictated by logic.

entries.name: Contests
entries: Sometimes one ship's or crewmember's efforts are directly opposed to another's. This can occur when both of them are trying to do the same thing and only one can succeed, such as attempting to pass through a narrow gap simultaneously. This situation also applies when one of them is trying to prevent the other one from accomplishing a goal—for example, when a ship's gravity projector tries to prevent another ship from jumping to hyperspace. In situations like these, the outcome is determined by a special form of ability check, called a contest.

Both participants in a contest make ability checks appropriate to their efforts. They apply all appropriate bonuses and penalties, but instead of comparing the total to a DC, they compare the totals of their two checks. The participant with the higher check total wins the contest. That ship or crewmember either succeeds at the action or prevents the other one from succeeding.

If the contest results in a tie, the situation remains the same as it was before the contest. Thus, one contestant might win the contest by default. If two ships tie in a contest to pass through a narrow gap, neither ship makes it. In a contest between a ship's gravity generator trying to prevent another ship from jumping to hyperspace, a tie means that the second ship fails to jump.

entries.name: Passive Checks
entries: A passive check is a special kind of ability check that doesn't involve any die rolls. Such a check can represent the average result for a task done repeatedly, such as probing meteors over and over, or can be used when the GM wants to secretly determine whether the characters succeed at something without rolling dice, such as noticing a hidden ship.

Here's how to determine a ship's total for a passive check: 10 + all modifiers that normally apply to the check. If the ship has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} on the check, add 5. For {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}, subtract 5. The game refers to a passive check total as a score.
For example. if a 1st-tier ship has a Wisdom of 15 and is proficiently equipped in Scan, it has a passive Wisdom (Scan) score of 13.

variantrule.name: Action
entries: You may take one action on your turn, and any action taken by a player with your ship can only be taken once per round unless otherwise stated. For example, although two different crewmembers could both cast the same {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} or make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check} with the {@skill Medicine|sw5e-phb} skill, they could not both take an action granted by a ship modification or the Boost Engines action, described below. Only the crewmember at the helm can take helm actions, but all other actions may be taken by anyone on the ship as logic dictates.

variantrule.name: Advantage
entries: Sometimes a special ability or power tells you that you have advantage or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check}, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}, or an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}. When that happens, you roll a second {@dice d20} when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have advantage, and use the lower roll if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}. For example, if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} and roll a 17 and a 5, you use the 5. If you instead have advantage and roll those numbers, you use the 17.

If multiple situations affect a roll and each one grants advantage or imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on it, you don't roll more than one additional {@dice d20}. If two favorable situations grant advantage, for example, you still roll only one additional {@dice d20}.

If circumstances cause a roll to have both advantage and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one {@dice d20}. This is true even if multiple circumstances impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} and only one grants advantage or vice versa. In such a situation, you have neither advantage nor {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}.

When you make a roll with advantage or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}, only the {@dice d20} is rolled twice. Any additional dice, such as the {@dice d4} granted by the {@i guidance} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, are only rolled once.

When you have advantage or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} and something in the game, such as the iktotchi's Precognition trait, lets you reroll the {@dice d20}, you can reroll only one of the dice. You choose which one. For example, if an iktotchi has advantage on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check} and rolls a 1 and a 13, the iktotchi could use the Precognition trait to reroll the 1.

You usually gain advantage or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} through the use of special abilities, actions, or powers. Inspiration (see chapter 4) can also give a character advantage on checks related to the character's personality, ideals, or bonds. The GM can also decide that circumstances influence a roll in one direction or the other and grant advantage or impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} as a result.

entries.name: Advantage on Other Rolls
entries: Though less common, advantage and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} can occur on other types of rolls as well. When you have advantage or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on a roll, as with a {@dice d20}, you roll the dice twice, using the higher of the two results with advantage, and using the lower of the two results if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}. If a roll has multiple dice, you roll the dice together and treat the results separately.

For instance, the Boost Weapons action potentially grants advantage on a ship damage roll once per turn. If any additional dice would be added to the damage roll, those additional dice are only rolled once.

variantrule.name: Armor Class
entries: Your Armor Class (AC) represents how well your starship avoids being damaged in battle—either my avoiding being hit entirely or by remaining essentially unharmed from an attack. Your AC is determined by four major factors: your base AC, your starship's Dexterity modifier, your ship's Tier bonuses, and the type of armor your ship has installed (see {@book Chapter 5: Equipment|sw5e-sotg|7|Chapter 5: Equipment} and {@book Chapter 4: Modifications|sw5e-sotg|6|Chapter 4: Modifications}).

Your ship has a base AC of 10. You then add (or subtract) the other factors above: Dexterity modifier, potentially limited by the type of armor you have installed; your ship's Tier bonus, if any; and any applicable modifications.

variantrule.name: Attack Roll
entries: When you make an attack with a primary or secondary weapon, your attack roll determines whether the attack hits or misses. To make an attack roll, roll a {@dice d20}, add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} (if you have at least one deployment rank), the ship's Wisdom modifier, and any weapon-specific bonuses or penalties. If the total of the roll plus modifiers equals or exceeds the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-sotg} (AC), the attack hits.
Ships are always considered proficiently equipped with their properly-installed weapons.

entries.name: Rolling 1 or 20
entries: Sometimes fate blesses or curses a gunner, causing the novice to hit and the veteran to miss.

If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 20, the attack hits regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC. In addition, the attack is a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-sotg|critical hit}, as explained later in this chapter.
If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 1, the attack misses regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC.

entries.name: Range
entries: You can make ranged attacks only against targets within a specified range.
Ship weaponry typically has two ranges. The value of these ranges depends on the type of weapon (primary, secondary, or tertiary), as described in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}.

entries.name: Ranged Attacks in Close combat
entries: Aiming a ranged attack is more difficult when a foe is next to you. When you make a ranged attack with a ship weapon, a power, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on the attack roll if you are within 50 feet of your target.

variantrule.name: Bonus Action
entries: Various class or deployment features, powers, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. You can only take a Bonus Action if some feature gives you one, and you can only take one Bonus Action on each of your turns.

variantrule.name: Cover
entries: Asteroids, ships, debris, and other obstacles can provide cover during starship combat, making a target more difficult to harm. A target can benefit from cover only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the cover.
There are four degrees of cover. If a target is behind multiple sources of cover, only the most protective degree applies; the degrees aren't added together.
A target with one-quarter cover has a +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}. A target has one-quarter cover if an obstacle blocks at least one-fourth of it.
A target with half cover has a +3 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}. A target has half cover if an obstacle blocks at least half of it.

A target with three-quarters cover has a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}. A target has three-quarters cover if about three-quarters of it is covered by an obstacle.

A target with total cover can't be targeted directly by an attack or a power, although some powers can reach such a target by including it in an area of effect. A target has total cover if it is completely concealed by an obstacle.

variantrule.name: Critical Hit
entries: When you score a critical hit, you get to roll extra dice for the attack's damage against the target. Roll all of the attack's damage dice twice and add them together. Then add any relevant modifiers as normal. To speed up play, you can roll all the damage dice at once.

variantrule.name: Destruction Saving Throw
entries: At the start of the ship's turn, if the ship has 0 {@variantrule Hull Points|sw5e-sotg|hull points}, you must make a special {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}, called a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}, to determine whether you can salvage your ship. Unlike other {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}, this one isn't tied to any ability score. Roll a {@dice d20}. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success has no effect by itself; on your third success, your ship becomes stable. On a failure, your ship suffers 1 level of {@condition System Damage|sw5e-sotg|system damage}.

{@b {@i Rolling 1 or 20.}} When you make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw} and roll a 1 on the {@dice d20}, it counts as two failures, causing 2 levels of {@condition System Damage|sw5e-sotg|system damage}. If you roll a 20 on the {@dice d20}, your ship regains 1 hull point.

{@b {@i Damage at 0 Hull Points.}} If your ship takes any damage while it has 0 {@variantrule Hull Points|sw5e-sotg|hull points}, it suffers 1 level of {@condition System Damage|sw5e-sotg|system damage}. If the damage is from a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-sotg|critical hit}, it suffers 2 levels instead. If the damage equals or exceeds its hull point maximum, it is instantly destroyed.

variantrule.name: Difficult Terrain
entries: Combat rarely takes place in featureless terrain. Asteroid fields, mountain ranges, other ships—the setting of a typical fight contains difficult terrain.
Every foot of movement in difficult terrain costs 1 extra foot. This rule is true even if multiple things in a space count as difficult terrain.

variantrule.name: Disadvantage
entries: Sometimes a special ability or power tells you that you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or disadvantage on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check}, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}, or an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}. When that happens, you roll a second {@dice d20} when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage}, and use the lower roll if you have disadvantage. For example, if you have disadvantage and roll a 17 and a 5, you use the 5. If you instead have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} and roll those numbers, you use the 17.

If multiple situations affect a roll and each one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or imposes disadvantage on it, you don't roll more than one additional {@dice d20}. If two favorable situations grant {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage}, for example, you still roll only one additional {@dice d20}.

If circumstances cause a roll to have both {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} and disadvantage, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one {@dice d20}. This is true even if multiple circumstances impose disadvantage and only one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or vice versa. In such a situation, you have neither {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} nor disadvantage.

When you make a roll with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or disadvantage, only the {@dice d20} is rolled twice. Any additional dice, such as the {@dice d4} granted by the {@i guidance} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, are only rolled once.

When you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or disadvantage and something in the game, such as the iktotchi's Precognition trait, lets you reroll the {@dice d20}, you can reroll only one of the dice. You choose which one. For example, if an iktotchi has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check} and rolls a 1 and a 13, the iktotchi could use the Precognition trait to reroll the 1.

You usually gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or disadvantage through the use of special abilities, actions, or powers. Inspiration (see chapter 4) can also give a character {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} on checks related to the character's personality, ideals, or bonds. The GM can also decide that circumstances influence a roll in one direction or the other and grant {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or impose disadvantage as a result.

entries.name: {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg} on Other Rolls
entries: Though less common, {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} and disadvantage can occur on other types of rolls as well. When you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or disadvantage on a roll, as with a {@dice d20}, you roll the dice twice, using the higher of the two results with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage}, and using the lower of the two results if you have disadvantage. If a roll has multiple dice, you roll the dice together and treat the results separately.

For instance, the Boost Weapons action potentially grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} on a ship damage roll once per turn. If any additional dice would be added to the damage roll, those additional dice are only rolled once.

variantrule.name: Expertise
entries: Certain features, such as Active Camouflage or a Boarding Harpoon, let your ship double its {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} with a given skill or modification, granting your ship the status of expertly equipped in that skill or modification. As usual, you can only gain expertly equipped status in a skill or modification once.

rows: push your ship to or beyond its limits
slam into an object to deal damage.
Sensor Dampener; {@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb} Device; {@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb} Device, Active Camouflage
allows the ship to remain undetected
attempt to regain {@variantrule Hull Points|sw5e-sotg|hull points}
pushed a ship beyond its natural limits
access data banks or process data
notice and locate the presence of objects
a general measurement of your ship's beauty and soundness
threaten via ship's appearance or abilities
pass your ship off as something it's not

variantrule.name: Firing Arc
entries: Ships have a firing arc, which is determined by the hardpoint on which they are mounted. Fixed hardpoints offer a limited firing arc, while turret hardpoints add an unlimited firing arc.

entries.name: Limited Firing Arc
entries: Many weapons can only fire in a single direction, indicated by a limited firing arc. The available arcs are spaced 90 degrees from each other and consist of: forward, aft, port, and starboard.
Weapons with a limited firing arc only fire at targets within a 90-degree arc, with the ship's center point as the arc's vertex.

entries.name: Unlimited Firing Arc
entries: Weapons with an unlimited firing arc can fire at any target within range and line of sight.

variantrule.name: Hull Points
entries: Hull points represent a ship's hull integrity. A ship's current hull points can be any number from its hull point maximum down to 0.
Whenever a ship takes damage, that damage is subtracted from its hull points. The loss of hull points has no effect on a ship's capabilities until the ship drops to 0 hull points.
At tier 0, hull points are determined by Hull Dice and the ship's Constitution modifier. Record hull point maximum, Hull Die type, and Hull Die count on the starship sheet.
Damage to hulls is permanent until repaired. When a ship receives repairs, hull points regained are added to its current hull points and can't exceed its hull point maximum.

variantrule.name: Initiative
entries: A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of cannon shots and ship maneuvers. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A {@b round} represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a {@b turn.} The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Each PC on a ship rolls initiative normally. The lowest initiative among PCs on a ship sets that ship's {@variantrule Ship Initiative|sw5e-sotg|initiative} for the round (see {@variantrule Ship Initiative|sw5e-sotg}).

variantrule.name: Making an Attack
entries: Whether you're firing laser cannons or a railgun, a starship attack follows these steps:
{@b 1. Choose a target.} Pick a target within your attack's range.
{@b 2. Determine modifiers.} The GM determines {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-sotg|cover}, {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage}, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage}.
{@b 3. Resolve the attack.} Make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll} or, for some weapons, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}; on a hit, roll damage.

entries.name: Attack Rolls
entries: Roll {@dice d20} + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} (if you have at least one deployment rank) + the ship's Wisdom modifier + weapon bonuses. The attack hits if the total meets or exceeds the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-sotg|AC}. Ships are proficient with properly installed weapons.
A natural 20 is a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-sotg|critical hit}; a natural 1 misses regardless of modifiers.
Ranged attacks with ship weapons have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} if you are within 50 feet of your target.

entries.name: Weapon Save DC
entries: Tertiary and quaternary weapons, and primary weapons on Huge and larger ships, often use a saving throw instead of an attack roll.
{@b Weapon save DC} = 8 + the crewmember's {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} (if at least rank 1) + the ship's Wisdom modifier.

When an effect grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on an attack that uses a save instead of an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}, the save is made with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} unless stated otherwise.
Add the ship's Strength modifier to damage from primary and secondary weapons.

variantrule.name: Proficiency
entries: Ships can be proficiently equipped for particular tasks, allowing her crew to add their Proficiency Bonus to the roll or save, as long as the crewmember has at least one deployment rank. Enemy ships also have this bonus, which is incorporated in their stat blocks. The bonus is used in the rules on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability checks}, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}, and {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack rolls}.

Your proficiency equipped bonus can't be added to a single die roll or other number more than once. For example, if two different rules say you can add your Proficiency Bonus to a Wisdom {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throw}, you nevertheless add the bonus only once when you make the save.

Occasionally, your Proficiency Bonus might be multiplied or divided (doubled or halved, for example) before you apply it. If a circumstance suggests that your Proficiency Bonus applies more than once to the same roll, you still add it only once and multiply or divide it only once.

By the same token, if a feature or effect allows you to multiply your Proficiency Bonus when making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-sotg|ability check} that wouldn't normally benefit from your Proficiency Bonus, you still don't add the bonus to the check. For that check your Proficiency Bonus is 0, given the fact that multiplying 0 by any number is still 0. For instance, if you are not proficiently equipped in the Data skill, you gain no benefit from a feature that lets you double your Proficiency Bonus when you make Intelligence (Data) checks.

In general, you don't multiply your Proficiency Bonus for {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack rolls} or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-sotg|saving throws}. If a feature or effect allows you to do so, these same rules apply.

entries.name: Expertly Equipped
entries: Certain features, such as Active Camouflage or a Boarding Harpoon, let your ship double its Proficiency Bonus with a given skill or modification, granting your ship the status of expertly equipped in that skill or modification. As usual, you can only gain expertly equipped status in a skill or modification once.

variantrule.name: Reaction
entries: Certain features allow you to take a Reaction. A Reaction is an instant response to a trigger of some kind, which can occur any turn.

When you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the Reaction interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction.

variantrule.name: Saving Throw
entries: A saving throw—also called a save—represents an attempt to resist a weapon effect, power, trap, or similar threat to your ship or crew. When a ship or crewmember is at risk, the GM may call for a save rather than an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}.

When you make a saving throw using your ship's abilities, roll a {@dice d20} and add the ship's relevant ability modifier. If your ship is proficiently equipped for that saving throw, also add the {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} of the crewmember at the helm.

While many weapons utilize an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}, tertiary and quaternary weapons, as well as primary weapons on Huge and larger ships, instead call for a saving throw. When an ability grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on an attack and the attack calls for a saving throw instead of an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-sotg|attack roll}, unless stated otherwise, the saving throw is made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} or {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage}, respectively. The saving throw is calculated as follows:
{@b Weapon save DC} = 8 + the crewmember's {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-sotg|Proficiency Bonus} (if at least rank 1) + the ship's Wisdom modifier

variantrule.name: Shield Points
entries: Many ships have shields—a buffer of energy measured in shield points in addition to hull points.
Whenever a ship with shield points takes damage, shields take the damage first. If damage reduces shield points to 0, the hull takes any remaining damage.

Shield point maximum and shield regeneration rate depend on shield dice, the ship's Strength modifier, and installed shield equipment (see {@book Chapter 5: Equipment|sw5e-sotg|7|Chapter 5: Equipment}).

variantrule.name: Ship Initiative
entries: Combat uses rounds and turns. During a round, each participant takes a turn; turn order is set by {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-sotg|initiative} at the start of the encounter.
Each PC on a ship rolls initiative normally. The {@b lowest} initiative among PCs on a ship sets that ship's initiative for the round.

On a ship's turn, the reactor replenishes power dice, the crew distributes them, and the crew may activate shield regeneration. All PCs on that ship then take individual turns in an order the crew agrees on (the helm breaks ties).

entries.name: NPC Ship Initiative
entries: For NPC ships, roll initiative as a Dexterity check modified by the ship's size:

variantrule.name: Space Versus Ground Scale
entries: Space combat uses scaled-down dice relative to ground combat. To convert between scales, multiply or divide damage, hull points, shield points, damage reduction, and shield regeneration by 10 as appropriate.

Large and larger ships may be immune to small-arms fire from individuals. Tiny starships are Tiny in space but Huge on the ground; Small ships are Gargantuan on the ground; Medium and larger ships are colossal.

Tiny–Large starships have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-sotg|disadvantage} on attacks against Large or smaller creatures; those creatures have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-sotg|advantage} on saves against such ships' weapons.

variantrule.name: Speed
entries: In combat, ships are in constant motion, often using movement and position to gain the upper hand.
On your turn, the crewmember at the helm can move the ship a distance up to its speed. The ship can use as much or as little of its speed as desired, following the rules here.
Starships come equipped with two speeds: flying speed and turning speed.
{@b Flying speed is how far your ship can travel in a single round. It is expressed in feet. For every foot your ship travels forward, it expends one foot from its speed.
A ship's unmodified flying speed is determined in {@book Chapter 3: Starships|sw5e-sotg|5|Chapter 3: Starships} by the Role selected for the ship at construction.

Turning speed determines how maneuverable your ship is. In order for your ship to rotate 90 degrees, you must spend an amount of your flying speed equal to your turning speed. For instance, if your ship has a flying speed of 350 feet, and a turning speed of 100 feet, you can travel 150 feet in a straight line, spending 150 feet of your flying speed, and then turn 90 degrees to starboard, spending 100 feet of your flying speed, leaving 100 feet of movement remaining.
Typically games are played with turning limited to 90 degree increments, but, if your group has the desire and capability to track smaller angles, this is allowed.
A ship can turn more (or less, if your group agrees) than 90 degrees on its turn, by spending a proportionate amount of movement.

If a ship's turning speed exceeds its flying speed, that ship cannot turn 90 degrees, in combat conditions, absent another effect modifiying the ship's turning speed and/or flying speed or the Hard Turn action.
A ship's unmodified turning speed is determined in {@book Chapter 3: Starships|sw5e-sotg|5|Chapter 3: Starships} by the Role selected for the ship at construction.

variantrule.name: Starship Damage Types
entries: Starship damage types differ slightly from ground combat. Notably, sonic damage does nothing in space.
{@b Acid}, {@b Cold}, and {@b Fire} deal half damage to shields.
{@b Energy} and {@b Force} deal normal damage to hull and shields.
{@b Ion} deals half damage to hull, cannot destroy ships outright—ion damage that would reduce a ship to 0 hull points instead leaves it {@condition Disabled|sw5e-sotg|disabled} and stable.
{@b Kinetic} deals normal damage; collisions deal kinetic damage.
{@b Lightning} deals half damage to hull.
{@b Necrotic} deals half damage to hull and shields.
{@b Poison} and {@b Psychic} deal no damage to ships.
{@b Sonic} deals normal damage in atmosphere but no damage in space.
{@b True} damage ignores effects that prevent or redirect damage.
